the degree of inequality and the generosity of the welfare state are both positively correlated with the degree of consensus in the political system, but that the degree of consensus is negatively correlated with the degree and type of inequality and positively correlated with the generosity of the social safety net.
the political economy of capitalism and inequality in the advanced countries is determined by the interaction between the political system and the economic system.
the varieties of capitalism and the political system are mutually reinforcing in generating different levels of inequality and welfare states.

understanding the role of economic and political institutions in the development of inequality and redistribution.
the relationship between the political and economic institutions that underpin the welfare states in advanced capitalist democracies.
the relationship between the political system and the economic system.

the institutional complementarities between varieties of capitalism and different political systems have a decisive influence on the distribution of incomes and the provision of social protection.
the welfare state and the distribution of incomes are not the result of economic and political forces operating independently of one another.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
inequality and redistribution are the outcome of the interaction of economic and political systems.

the institutional structure and the political economy of the advanced economies have evolved into different varieties of capitalism and politics, with the former reinforcing the latter in generating different degrees of economic inequality and welfare states.
the political system is the main driver of welfare regimes, while capitalism shapes inequality and poverty.
The main takeaway from our work is that
inequality and redistribution are endogenous to the political economy of capitalism, and that the institutional complementarities that generate these results are not easily amenable to policy change.
the institutional complementarity of political and economic systems is key in explaining inequality and welfare state outcomes.
the role of politics is crucial in understanding the persistence and the variation of inequality and welfare states.
